cim: The CMA says Meta made changes to Muse's ToS in the UK to reflect the country's consumer law; the terms give users far more protections than in the US (Joseph Bambridge/Politico)
cim_eredeti: The CMA says Meta made changes to Muse's ToS in the UK to reflect the country's consumer law; the terms give users far more protections than in the US (Joseph Bambridge/Politico)
szoveg_eredeti:
LONDON — Meta will be on the hook for more of Muse’s mistakes in the U.K. than in the U.S., according to a comparison of the AI agent's fine print in both countries by POLITICO.

Following conversations with regulators, Muse’s terms of service give British consumers more scope to seek redress if the personal AI agent makes mistakes compared with users in the U.S.

The findings indicate the tech giant was willing to commit to meeting higher liability standards to gain access to the U.K. market, and show that tech companies and users will face different liability and consumer law rules as personal AI agents roll out globally.

Muse, an AI agent that takes actions on users’ behalf, was introduced in the U.K. this week — several months after its launch in the U.S. — following talks with British regulators.

The Competition and Markets Authority, which enforces consumer law in the U.K., said Meta had made changes to Muse’s terms of service in the U.K. following “weeks” of engagement to “make them fairer for consumers” and ensure they reflect U.K. consumer law.

Meta declined to comment on detailed regulatory discussions. It says Muse can lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping — but publicly acknowledges the tool “can and will still make mistakes.”

The AI agent, which is the first to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., can also make payments on behalf of users with their approval.

The U.S. terms of service cap liability at $250 except for claims “arising from Meta’s gross negligence, willful misconduct or fraud.”

They absolve Meta of liability “to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law” for any losses or damages caused by Muse “taking any unintended, erroneous or unauthorized action.”

In the U.K. there is no financial cap and a narrower list of exceptions to Meta’s liability applies only where the company has “acted with reasonable skill and care / professional diligence.”

Under U.K. consumer law, this standard is automatically implied into contracts for services between a business and a consumer. How U.K. consumers would fare in practice when seeking redress for any problems caused by personal AI agents is yet to be tested in court.

Since its debut in the U.S., Meta staffers have reportedly raised concerns internally about “undesired actions” by the agent, from accessing encrypted messages to supplying bogus information about purchases. (A Meta spokesperson said these were “isolated incidents.”)

The CMA said it expects Muse to be the first of many personal AI agents to come to the U.K. and has invited users to report any issues they experience with personal AI agents.

Other British regulators are also watching closely. The Financial Conduct Authority said in a statement that as AI agents become capable of making transactions, payments and investment decisions, companies developing and deploying them “must understand which activities require authorisation and where regulatory requirements may apply.”

It also highlighted that a broad Consumer Duty could also apply to regulated firms’ use of AI agents, and that all companies must decide carefully whether they should accept payments initiated by an agent.

As well as contract law, consumer law, negligence and sector-specific regulation, users of AI agents may soon also be able to seek redress through product liability laws.

The Law Commission is reviewing the U.K.’s product liability laws and has proposed extending the definition to software, including AI. Doing so could make firms developing or deploying AI agents strictly liable for certain types of harm they cause.
